1991.dq: Stress is used as a criterion to define the phonological word. Generally speaking, a phonological word contains just one primary stress. The primary stress in Usen Barok almost always falls on the final syllable of a phonological word (with a few exceptions). [p. 56] ... A phonological word is defined as containing only one primary stress. See §2.9. [fn. 20, p. 117]
1991.dloc: Ch. 2 'Phonology and phonetics', sec. 2.9 'Stress', thesis pp. 56-58 (Table 2-15 p. 57; exx. (2-37)-(2-40) pp. 57-58); ch. 1 typological overview p. 15; sec. 1.2 p. 9 (Garrett 1999a:3 cited); fn. 20 p. 117 (phonological word = one primary stress); sec. 2.3.8 'Vowels' (allophony) p. 31 (kaunoon [kau.'no:n] 'clam shell', diphthong in a non-final syllable passed over); sec. 2.5 (diphthong = one syllable, one peak); ch. 5 sec. 5.4.1.5 p. 137, passage before ex. (5-37) (ine NP marker vs 3SG pronoun); ch. 10 p. 260, after ex. (10-59) (stripped nouns keep their own stress)
1991.prule: Primary stress on the final (ultimate) syllable of the phonological word; one primary stress per phonological word. The rule is stated with no weight condition and the corpus examples ignore weight: closed non-final syllables are passed over for a light final (bunbunnarama [bun.ˌbun.na.ra.'ma], ex. 2-37), a closed root-final syllable loses primary stress to a following enclitic (xiset /γi.'set/ > xisetsik /ˌγi.set.'sik/, ex. 2-39), and a diphthong in a non-final syllable is passed over (kaunoon [kau.'no:n] 'clam shell', sec. 2.3.8 p. 31; sec. 2.5 states that a diphthong is one syllable with one peak). The source gives no example of a long vowel in a non-final syllable (every long vowel in stress-marked forms sits in the stressed final syllable, e.g. [pa.'ma:], [ka.'mi:], [lɔ.'γɔ:n]), so for long vowels quantity-insensitivity rests on the unconditioned statement alone. Secondary stress on the first syllable of 3- and 4-syllable words.

1993.prule: No positional stress rule. Stress (= loudness) is a concomitant of high tone: every high-toned syllable is stressed, every low syllable is unstressed. Each single-root stem carries at most one lexically contrastive H, on the final or the penultimate syllable, or none (patterns LL, HL, LH on the last two syllables; monosyllables low; most disyllables all-low). Further Hs are derived by perturbation (after a low root/stem/word the first vowel of the next unit becomes H; Hs never on adjacent syllables within a word, may sit on alternate syllables). The only tone-independent stress is a non-contrastive utterance-initial stress with semi-high pitch.

1993.tone: The source treats the system as tone: three contrastive stem tone patterns (LL, HL, LH) on the last two syllables of single-root stems, at most one H per root, minimal pairs (e.g. naanga 'big' vs naanga 'older sister', p.284), further Hs by perturbation. Stress is defined as loudness and is strictly a property of H syllables ('High-tone syllables are also stressed... Other syllables are low (unmarked) and unstressed', p.283). Vowel length is inherent per vowel quality (aa/e/o two moras, i/u one and a half, a one, ɨ shorter) and unaffected by H/stress. Lloyd 1969 (PL A-22, p.32) describes the same facts as 'pitch-accent': 'three basic pitch-accent patterns on noun stems. Most have no pitch-accent, while others have pitch-accent on either the ultimate or penultimate syllable', with a morphotonemic rule adding a pitch-accent to the first syllable of a word/root/morpheme unless the following syllable or either of the two preceding syllables has a basic one. Lloyd 1992 (PL C-82, intro) says 'certain syllables are emphasised by loudness and high tone... In a number of cases the tone difference gives the only contrast between two words'. Privative-H / pitch-accent and tone are both defensible labels; either way there is no positional stress rule.

2000.srule: Exists, placement not given: Adams says the root syllable stays strongest 'auch neben einem anderen sekundären Akzent' (even alongside another, secondary accent) but gives no rule or examples for where a secondary accent falls.
2000.quote: III. Wortton. Der Ton ruht für gewöhnlich auf der vorletzten Silbe. Bei zusammengesetzten Formen kann er bis auf die drittletzte Silbe beibehalten werden. Wörter, welche nur infolge des Präfixes (Vorsilbe) zweisilbig sind, behalten den Ton naturgemäß auf ihrer Stammsilbe; z. B. diké Ei; dibé Euter, weibliche Brust. Die Grundregel für die Wortbetonung ist also: die Wurzelsilbe der Grundform bleibt immer die starke, kräftige Silbe des Wortgebildes, auch neben einem anderen sekundären Akzent.

2000.tone: Adams 1907 is a pre-tonological missionary description that uses 'Ton'/'Betonung'/'Akzent' for word stress and does not recognise tone; his acute also marks vowels that are 'kurz, geschlossen und betont' (p. 37, I. Vokale). The two modern descriptions held in the copy consulted describe Banɔ'ɔ as a two-tone language and say nothing about stress: Den Besten 2016 (Leiden MA, ch. 6 'Tone', pp. 38-41: 'Tone in Bano'o has contrastive function', minimal pairs è̩ɓɔ́jí 'crazy' / è̩ɓɔ̩̀jí 'frame'; p. 51 'Bano'o has two tones, high and low') and Kouankem 2003 (sec. 2.1.2 'Tones': 'There are two lexical tones in Banoo, high and low which contrast in identical environments'). Adams's stem-initial 'strong syllable' may partly reflect stem-initial H tone/prominence rather than stress in the modern sense; the modern sources neither confirm nor deny word stress.

2003.prule: Main (dynamic) word accent falls on the stem syllable (Stammsilbe); every non-stem syllable (prefix, derivational or inflectional suffix, reduced compound member) is weaker, on a four-grade strength scale. The position is fixed by morphological structure (Germanic root stress), not by syllable count or syllable weight.
2003.srule: Non-stem syllables carry a graded secondary stress (Nebenton, grades 2-3 of Lessiak's four). Its strength and place depend on (a) the syllable cut of the stem syllable (a weakly cut, long-vowel stem depresses the next syllable more); (b) the syllable's own vowel: schwa or syllabic nasal/liquid = unaccented (grade 4), full-vowel syllables (e.g. -ig, -lich, -in, -ung, -sam, -fach, -haft, -schaft, -bar, -keit; alle, ente, uhu) = 'unterstark' (grade 3); (c) rhythm: in a trisyllable with an unstressed second syllable the third takes the Nebenaccent (1:4:3a); a heavy suffix in second position before a weak third takes it instead (about 1:3:4); a heavy suffix in third position always outranks the second (1:4a:3); with a further non-stem syllable the first is weak and the second carries the Nebenaccent (1a:4:3b:4). Compound second members carry a Nebenton (§ 46, see morphology note).

2010.tone: Two-level mora-based tone (High vs toneless), one H maximum per word, H realized as High-falling; the author adopts Odden's (1988) 'predictable tone system' label and states H position is constant in isolation and in sentences. She contrasts Bena's tonal system with Swahili's stress-based one and notes, impressionistically, a compressed H/L pitch range in younger speakers as a possible incipient tone-to-stress transition under Swahili influence. 2012.prule: Bende is described as a tone language (lexically and grammatically distinctive tone; H and L basic, with R and F as realisations of LH/HL on one syllable). Every noun stem / verb root belongs to one of three lexical tonal types (2006: H-type, L-type, 0-type; 2021: patterns (a) stem all H, (b) prefix H + stem beginning L/R, (c) prefix L + H (or R/F containing H) on the stem penult, final L; thesis Tone Rule 1 by stem syllable count 1σ/2σ/3σ/4σ+: H-type H/HH/HHH/HHHH, L-type R/LH/LHH/LHHH, 0-type R/RL~HL/LHL/LLHL). No word-stress or accent rule is stated; the terms 強勢/アクセント/stress are never applied to Bende.
2012.quote: 本稿では、名詞および動詞の声調について、引用形で観察される声調のパターンを整理する。句や文での声調については未調査である。... ベンデ語の声調は、決して例は多くないが、語彙的および文法的弁別機能を持つ。音節ごとに高声調 H(igh)、低声調 L(ow)、上昇声調 R(ising)、下降声調 F(alling) の 4 種類の実現声調があるが、本稿では名詞の引用形、動詞の動名詞形を基に、いくつかの環境を設定してどのようなパターンあるか観察する。その結果、ベンデ語の声調は、音節数が増えてもパターンが限定的であり、基本的には 3 パターンである。すなわち、(a) 語幹がすべて H、(b) 接頭辞は H で語幹が L あるいは R ではじまるもの、(c) は接頭辞が L で語幹の次末音節に H ないし H を含む R や F が現れるものである。 [Abe 2021: 249] — [thesis p. 57] ベンデ語も大多数の Bantu 諸語と同様, 意味の区別に弁別的な声調を持つ. [p. 59] 語幹ないし語根の声調型には 3 種類あり, それぞれ H(igh) 型, L(ow) 型, 0 型と呼ぶことにする. H 型は語幹ないし語根が H で始まるもの, L 型は語幹ないし語根が L で始まるもの, 0 型は後ろから 2 番目の音節が H となり最終音節は再び L となるも…

2012.tone: Neither source mentions stress or accent for Bende: in the 2021 chapter アクセント occurs once, only in the footnote naming the ILCAA project 'アフリカ諸語における声調・アクセントの総合的研究'; 強勢/ストレス/stress/accent/卓立/プロミネンス: 0 hits (a full-text search of the layer). The thesis TOC and ch. 3 (声調) have no accent/stress heading. The penultimate H of the 0-type / pattern (c) — which absorbs most Swahili loans and prefixless words such as ʧǎi 'tea' — is one of three lexical tone classes, not a stress; H-type words are all H and L-type words have no penult prominence. Vowel length is contrastive (thesis p. 30, per source list: long vowels only from lexical length and V+V concatenation, i.e. no penultimate lengthening). Constraints noted: R/F only on long vowels or CG syllables; syllabic-less nasal prefixes cannot bear H (the H shifts to the last syllable of the preceding word, e.g. onto copula ni); after an L (copula ni, L-initial stems) an H stretch lasts only two syllables (open problem, p. 276); two finite conjugations neutralise the three classes to L.

tn.quote: 声調を担う単位 (Tone Bearing Unit: TBU) は、基本的に音節 ((N)C(G))V(V) である。... 以上のように、(C)V の V が短母音の場合には R や F は現れず、長母音や子音とわたり音の連続 (CG) の前後など音節が長めに発音される音節のみに H が遅めに実現される R や HL が 1 つの音節で実現されて F となるなど、出現は予測可能である。このことから、ベンデ語には基本的には H と L の 2 種類の声調があるが、音節の種類によって R や F と実現されうる。つまり、ベンデ語の R や F は、中国語などの R や F のように H や L に対立する弁別的な声調ではない。
tn.translation: The tone-bearing unit (TBU) is basically the syllable ((N)C(G))V(V). ... As shown above, R and F do not appear when the V of (C)V is a short vowel; their occurrence is predictable: only on syllables pronounced longer, such as long vowels or before/after a consonant+glide sequence (CG), is H realised late as R, or HL realised on one syllable as F. Hence Bende basically has two tones, H and L, which depending on syllable type may be realised as R or F. That is, Bende R and F are not distinctive tones opposed to H and L like the R and F of e.g. Chinese.
